### From one-way analysis to GLM

One-way analysis is definitely useful, but it has its limits:

-   Variables used in one-way analysis can be correlated (e.g. young
    drivers tend to drive powerful cars), so their one-way effects
    partly count the same risk twice.
-   It does not tell us which variables are the best to describe /
    predict the target.
-   It cannot quantify the independent influence of correlated
    variables on the target.

This is where the multi-way approach comes in. Multi-way analysis looks
at all the variables **at the same time** and is usually done with a
statistical or machine learning model. In insurance, when we want a very
transparent and easily interpretable model, we usually use the
Generalized Linear Model - **GLM**. It was introduced in the Lesson 4
support material (`Lesson4/Support/02_glm_motivation.md`), here is a
short recap.

A GLM generalizes the well-known linear regression in two ways:

1.  **Distribution** - the target does not have to be normal. Typical
    choices in insurance are Poisson for claim counts (frequency), Gamma
    for claim amounts (severity) and Tweedie for amounts with many zeros
    (burning cost). The Tweedie distribution is controlled by the power
    parameter `p`; for `1 < p < 2` it is a compound of Poisson and Gamma
    (a random number of claims, each with a Gamma-distributed size).
    Our target is the burning cost (loss per unit of exposure) - it has
    a lot of zeros and a long right tail - so we use Tweedie with
    `p = 1.5` as a good default.
2.  **Link function** - the linear combination of variables is connected
    to the expected target through a link function. We use the **log
    link**, so the effects of the variables get **multiplied**: base
    price x multiplier of variable 1 x multiplier of variable 2 ...

More details on Wikipedia: [GLM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_linear_model),
[Tweedie distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tweedie_distribution).

A reminder of the units we prepared in Lesson 4:

-   `Time_Exposure` - length of the policy as a fraction of a year, in
    (0, 1]
-   `Burning_Cost` - loss per policy-year (`Ult_Loss / Time_Exposure`)
-   `Ult_Loss` - `Paid + Reserves` (incurred loss, without IBNR)

```{r cell_02}
# install.packages(c("statmod", "tweedie"))
library(statmod)
library(tweedie)
library(dplyr)

dt_pol_w_claims <- readRDS("/cloud/project/Data/dt_pol_w_claims_target.rds") |>
  filter(!(is.na(Veh_type2) | Veh_type2 == ""))

table(dt_pol_w_claims$Veh_type2)
```

### Categorical predictors

A GLM works with numbers, so how does it use a category like the vehicle
type? A category has no order or distance (a TRUCK is not "3 x CAR"), so
we cannot just put numbers 1, 2, 3 ... into the model. Instead, each
category becomes its own 0/1 **indicator (dummy) variable** - "is this
vehicle a MOTORBIKE?", "is it a TRUCK?" ... One category is left out as
the **baseline** - it is the case when all the indicators are 0 and it is
absorbed by the intercept. This is what the model actually sees:

```{r cell_03}
head(model.matrix(~ Veh_type2, data = dt_pol_w_claims), 6)
```

Each indicator gets its own coefficient - its own multiplier relative to
the baseline - so the model does not assume any shape across the
categories. Every category can have any riskiness. That is also why a
categorical variable usually fits the data very well.

#### Banding of numeric variables

A numeric variable (e.g. driver age) gets only **one** coefficient. With
the log link this means a constant percentage change per unit, for
example "+1% risk with every additional year of age" - the relationship
is forced to be a smooth, one-directional curve. Real relationships are
often not like that, e.g. both very young and very old drivers can be
riskier than the middle-aged ones.

That is why numeric variables are often **banded** first - cut into
intervals which are then treated as categories, with one multiplier per
band. This lets the model follow a non-linear (even non-monotonic)
pattern. The data already contain such a variable, `D_age_banded`. This
is how banding looks like:

```{r cell_04}
dt_pol_w_claims |>
  filter(!is.na(D_age)) |>
  mutate(D_age_band = cut(D_age, breaks = c(0, 30, 40, 50, 60, Inf))) |>
  group_by(D_age_band) |>
  summarize(
    exposure = sum(Time_Exposure),
    burning_cost = weighted.mean(Burning_Cost, Time_Exposure)
  )
```

Banding has its price: more parameters and less data in every band, so
the multipliers get noisier. We have to find a balance - and we will
come back to banding and merging of categories in Exercise 3.

### Basic GLM

Let's fit a basic GLM using a single variable - Veh_type2. This will get
results very similar to the one-way analysis.

```{r cell_05}
basic_model <- glm(
  data = dt_pol_w_claims,
  formula = Burning_Cost ~ Veh_type2,
  family = statmod::tweedie(var.power = 1.5, link.power = 0),
  weights = Time_Exposure
)

summary(basic_model)
```

The most basic information we want to get from the model are the
coefficients. Since vehicle type is a categorical variable, each of its
categories is fitted as a separate variable (the indicators from above)
and we get a separate coefficient for each of them.

```{r cell_06}
summary(basic_model)$coef
summary(basic_model)$coef[, 1]
```

These coefficients are a little bit hard to interpret as they are now.
Linear regression's coefficients are expressed in the units of the
target variable. They represent the average increase / decrease of the
target given 1 unit change in the input variable.

On the other hand, GLM uses a link function - a transformation which
allows us to use a linear combination of predictors to estimate a
non-linear target. This transformation is not applied on the target but
on the linear combination of predictors.

We defined the target distribution as
`statmod::tweedie(var.power = 1.5, link.power = 0)` and used
`link.power = 0`, which represents the logarithmic link function. Now
that we know the link function, we can use the inverse link function
(exponential function in our case) to obtain more interpretable
coefficients.

While the coefficients don't signify the average increase or decrease,
their interpretation is even better. The intercept gets translated to
the expected target (burning cost) of the baseline category, and the
variable coefficients get translated into multipliers - signifying how
much riskier a category is than the baseline.

```{r cell_07}
weighted.mean(dt_pol_w_claims$Burning_Cost, dt_pol_w_claims$Time_Exposure)

summary(basic_model)$coef[, 1] |>
  exp() |>
  round(3)
```

As you can see, the CAR category is gone. This is because the most
populated category gets designated as the baseline category, which is
included within the intercept. The intercept (about 241) is therefore
the expected burning cost of a personal CAR, which is close to, but not
the same as, the overall weighted mean above.

The other coefficients (multipliers) represent how much each vehicle
type category is riskier than a personal car. For example, the MOTORBIKE
vehicle type is about 45% less risky than the personal CAR (multiplier
0.55). On the other hand, the TRUCK category is about 67% riskier than
the personal CAR (multiplier 1.67).

You may also notice multipliers of exactly 0 for OTHER and TRACTOR.
These categories have a very small exposure (only 5 and 21 policies) and
no losses at all, so the model happily says "zero risk", which is
obviously not credible. We will deal with such categories in Exercise 3
by merging them.

Did you expect this kind of result or are you surprised? Don't forget
the riskiness includes not only the aspect of claim loss payments but
also how often these claims occur.
